cultivar: Fenghuang Shui Xian, Huang Zhi Xiang strain
processing: Sun-withered, shaken overnight to a medium-light oxidation, fixed, rolled into long strips and charcoal roasted light to medium, usually in two passes for high-mountain lots.
harvest_season: Spring, April into early May; a mid-season strain picked once, with the Wudong lots last and most prized.
appearance_dry: Long, straight, slightly glossy dark brown strips with a bright floral smell.
appearance_wet: Long, thick yellow-green leaves with even red edges.
taste_profile: A strong gardenia aroma with a touch of citrus blossom, a medium-full body with honey and ripe fruit, a gentle roast and a long, cooling mineral finish.

brewing.notes: Boiling water, thin gaiwan, flash steeps. Strong enough to carry a slightly slower pour than Ya Shi Xiang, but still decant completely every time.

vintage_note: Sold by harvest year, spring tea on sale from around June for lighter roasts and from autumn for medium roasts and Wudong lots; it keeps two to four years sealed and dry, and old-tree lots are among the dancongs sometimes sold a year or two after harvest with the year stated.
description:
Huang Zhi Xiang, gardenia fragrance, is one of the backbone strains of Phoenix dancong: widely planted, strongly aromatic and the type that the most famous old trees on Wudong belong to. If Mi Lan Xiang is the honey of the family, this is the flowers, with a gardenia note that is unmistakable once you have met it.

The name is written with the characters for yellow branch but refers to the gardenia (huang zhi), and the strain is counted among the ten classic aroma types. It descends from selected single trees of the Fenghuang Shui Xian population above Chaozhou, and it matters historically because the celebrated Song Zhong tree at Li Zai Ping on Wudong, which died in 2016, was a Huang Zhi Xiang; much tea sold as Song Zhong is this type from old trees.

The leaf is withered, shaken overnight to a medium-light oxidation, rolled into strips and charcoal roasted, with high-mountain lots usually roasted lightly in two passes. In the cup the gardenia aroma comes first, with a hint of citrus blossom, then a medium-full body with honey and ripe fruit, a gentle toastiness and a long, cool, mineral finish; good Wudong lots have the mountain-rhyme depth that Chaozhou drinkers prize.

Brew it like every dancong, lots of leaf, boiling water, instant pours and full decanting; it has enough structure to survive a slightly slow hand and runs eight steeps with the middle ones the best. It is a good tea for food and a good first high-mountain dancong because its character is easy to read.

It is sold by year with the village and elevation stated by any serious seller, from everyday high-mountain tea to Wudong old-tree lots at serious prices. Keep it sealed, drink lighter roasts within two years, and when you are ready, taste it next to a Song Zhong from the same seller to understand exactly what old trees add to the same aroma.
history:
Huang Zhi Xiang is the gardenia type of Phoenix dancong. Its best-known line runs back to the Song Zhong tree at Liziping, at about 1150 metres. Local legend ties the Song Zhong name to the end of the Southern Song, and that age has not been proven.

The usual account of that tree gives a run of names: tuan shu ye for the shape of its leaf, then da ye xiang. In 1946 an overseas Chinese tea house in Vietnam sold it as yan shang zhen, and after the Wudong cooperative refined it in 1956 tasters noted the gardenia scent and it took the name Huang Zhi Xiang.

Villagers took cuttings in 1962, which helped the type spread. The old tree, reported to be over 700 years old, died in 2016, and it is now kept at a dancong museum in Chaozhou.
